title: Cocaine crime ring smashed in Edmonton: Armoured police raid: Probe launched after shoot-out with 'Crazy Jimmy': [All But Toronto Edition]
article: Edmonton police said a major organized crime group specializing in cocaine was dismantled yesterday, concluding an investigation started a year ago after police shot and killed a gang enforcer known as "Crazy Jimmy."

The top level of an organization that may have had inter- provincial connections was arrested after heavily-armoured police officers raided 20 houses and a business in and around Edmonton, police said.

Seven people were arrested, including Minh Cao Nguyen, and his wife, Le Vinh Nguyen, as well as her father, Thanh Ke Lam, who are alleged to be at the top of the group's hierarchy and are all charged with conspiracy to traffic in cocaine.

"We believe that their main source of revenue was trafficking cocaine. Their existence came to light a year ago and we have been pursuing them through this investigation for the past year," said Annette Bidniak, spokeswoman for the Edmonton Police Service.
"We believe we have pretty much taken the top off of the group. We believe one of the people we have arrested was the supplier and the others were the top rungs."

Although officers were still tallying the results of seizures made in their raids, Ms. Bidniak said the small amount of cocaine found -- about five ounces, which is worth about $7,500 on the street -- does not reflect the importance of the organization.

"It doesn't seem like a lot in terms of the amount seized; it doesn't necessarily compare to what is being passed by these people through their organization. For us, it is well worth the effort if we dismantle this group and cripple their operation because it is far more difficult to do business when you're in jail."
Throughout the probe, an additional 40 ounces of cocaine and nearly $162,000 of cash were also seized, she said. Three handguns were found yesterday, one of them a replica pistol.
"It is really a multi-ethnic group," said Ms. Bidniak.

"More and more we're seeing what you can call hybrid organizations because while it appears it is Asian-based because at the top end of the ladder the people are of Asian descent, but right within the top part of the organization you have a variety of ethnicities.
"You work with the people who will make you money," she said.

The investigation by Edmonton police and the RCMP started after police received information related to the shooting death of Long Duy Hoang, an enforcer for a notorious Edmonton crime gang, who earned the nickname "Crazy Jimmy" through a liberal use of violence.
He died of multiple gunshot wounds after a shoot-out with police last year.
"He shot at our officers and they returned fire and he was killed. It was shortly after that that information on some of these people came to light.
"That doesn't mean these people were directly working with Crazy Jimmy. We don't believe they are," said Ms. Bidniak.
"They knew each other. They all have been associated for a long time." She declined to say what the link between the cases was.
It is not surprising that the investigation was sparked by a shooting, said an organized crime specialist.
"People attract police attention usually because of violence," said James Dubro, author of several books on organized crime, including one exploring Asian gangs in Canada.
Asian-based organized crime has been evolving in Alberta since the late 1970s, he said.

"It doesn't have the history when compared to Vancouver, Montreal or Toronto. The Edmonton stuff doesn't really start until the late 1970s when they had Triad activity with gangs involved in heroin trafficking.
"Then the street gangs got going in the 1980s. The last couple of years it has been really active," said Mr. Dubro.
There are many highly-mobile Chinese and Vietnamese gangs operating in Western Canada.
They should be distinguish from the much fewer and less visible Triad and Big Circle Boys groups who operate at a much more sophisticated level with important international connections, he said.
